name: Ben Mensah

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I am with the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to employers, AI firms, unions or government, and your answers are confidential. What fills a normal shift?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I lead the underground drill crew at Red Lantern mine and run the jumbo drill on the hard faces. My two-year technical diploma got me started, but listening to the drill through the rock took years. My partner and I have grown children, good savings and a pension date we are beginning to discuss. I use AI every day to group drill faults before the morning check, then compare the list with the machine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the crew that small improvements to fault notes are welcome. I already use AI to group them, and I would like to test its new bit-wear chart. The face still needs an operator who can hear a bit pull sideways.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My job and pay look secure. We have over six months of expenses saved and several mines within reach, so I would not rush a career change. I would still compare the chart with the physical bit because neat numbers can be wrong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep drilling and test the new AI bit-wear chart against removed bits for four weeks. I would mark every wrong warning and show the mechanic. I would leave our pension contribution schedule as it is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm and curious. I like a tool that shortens the morning check without moving responsibility off the crew.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What wrong warning would matter most?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A chart that says a bit is sound when its edge has chipped. I would photograph the edge and enter the actual wear. A clean chart cannot hold a broken drill bit together.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you put your own money into the tool?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, it is mine equipment and the mine can fund a trial. Our savings are for retirement and household choices. I can offer my time and records.

think: My **job and pay** look secure, supported by substantial savings and nearby mines.
A neat **AI chart** still needs physical checks for chipped bits.
do: **Test** the new AI bit-wear chart against removed bits for four weeks.
feel: **Calm** and curious about a practical tool.

fieldNote: He uses **AI daily**, and the new action is testing a bit-wear feature.
Strong **savings**, high pay and local options support a calm mood.
He keeps **physical inspection** with the crew despite enjoying new tools.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say buying and planning will change before the jumbo drill runs itself. I would offer to test AI hole plans with the surveyor. The drill crew and office should both see the errors before targets change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My own wage looks sound while robots move slowly, but the surveying team could lose hours. A faster plan could also push a crew to skip checking cracked rock. I would feel responsible if my name went on a bad pattern.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would learn the new AI hole-planning screen with the surveyor over two weeks. I would compare three planned faces with the rock and log every changed hole. If management set targets without those corrections, I would ask for a joint crew review.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy for the surveyors and for safety, though I still expect to keep my pay. I would rather test a plan than argue about the idea of one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which hole would you change first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The one beside a crack at shoulder height. I would show the surveyor where the drill bit starts to pull. A plan can be fast and still put a hole in the wrong rock.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a joint review involve?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The drill crew, surveyor and shift manager would see the same marked pattern. We would decide who signs off before the blast. I would want that rule written down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the crew that full thinking AI by 2028 changes drill plans first, while capable robot drills appear around 2031. The mine might buy them, and we should test a machine in real rock before cutting posts. I would ask for a written trial plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be sixty when thinking AI arrives and sixty-three when robots become capable. If Red Lantern bought robot drills in 2031, I might lose my high wage earlier than planned. We have savings, but I would not assume the same work exists at other mines.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would pause the plan to replace our second car and request pension figures for retiring at sixty-three and sixty-five. I would keep drilling after 2028 while people still work the faces. If the mine posted a paid robot-test role and funded training, I would enrol while keeping my wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but not lost. I can run a trial and price retirement, yet I cannot promise a paid seat will remain.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the robot test have to include?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A hard face with a hidden crack, not a showroom wall. I would log stops and near misses beside the machine. A robot drill trial on easy rock would answer the wrong question.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you move to another mine?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would call and ask whether it had bought robot drills before applying. A current vacancy would not guarantee work in 2031. I would make the move only for a real paid offer.

say: I would separate **2028 thinking AI** from capable robot drills around 2031.
I would require **real-rock trials** before any drill posts are cut.
think: At **sixty-three**, a robot purchase could end my high wage before planned retirement.
Savings help, but **nearby vacancies** may also change when robots arrive.
do: **Pause** replacing the second car and request pension figures for ages sixty-three and sixty-five.

S2.quote: A robot drill trial on easy rock would answer the wrong question.
fieldNote: He distinguishes **2028 plans** from capable robot drills around 2031.
Strong savings allow a **retirement calculation**, but do not erase possible lost wages.
Training requires a **funded place**, posted paid test role and continued wages.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say five years to thinking AI and roughly eight to capable robot drills gives us a fair chance to test equipment and plan retirement. I would ask for a published safety-trial calendar. The drill crew should set the stop rules.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be sixty-three when thinking AI arrives in 2031 and about sixty-six when capable robots arrive in 2034. Our pension may let me retire by then, but I would check monthly income before deciding. If I stayed, I could help run the robot safety trials.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would pilot a new AI drill-risk map with the surveyor this winter and compare it with actual fault logs. I would ask for pension projections at sixty-five and sixty-seven. If Red Lantern posted a paid safety-trial role with funded instruction, I would take it while still earning my drill wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about the younger crew, steadier about my own options. Eight years lets me test the map and our income plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you mark on the risk map?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The crack that opened behind the third drill last spring. I would ask the crew to check whether the map flags it before drilling. A coloured warning is only useful if it matches the wall.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if retirement is affordable at sixty-five?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My partner and I might choose that date, even if I enjoy the safety trials. I would not promise a trial team more years than I wanted to work. I would hand over the fault log to a younger operator.

I would let the **drill crew** set stop rules.
think: At about **sixty-six**, retirement may be affordable if pension income covers bills.
A paid **trial role** remains an option if I keep working.

**Compare** pension projections at sixty-five and sixty-seven with bills.
**Take** funded trial instruction if a paid role opens and wages continue.
feel: **Uneasy** for younger crew members, steadier about his own path.
S3.quote: A coloured warning is only useful if it matches the wall.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say a decade before thinking AI and roughly thirteen years before capable robot drills gives the mine time to test properly. I would ask it to publish the calendar and train younger operators. I could help write the handover notes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be sixty-eight in 2036 and about seventy-one when capable robots arrive in 2039. I expect to retire before then if our pension stays on course. Our savings make that likely, though I would still review the numbers each year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep leading drills for now and write down the fault sounds I teach apprentices. I would request an annual pension update and review it with my partner. I would offer the notes to a junior operator before leaving the crew.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm about our own income path and interested in leaving good records. A long warning gives us choices.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you stay just to see the robot drills?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe for a demonstration, but I would not delay retirement for one. My partner and I have plans outside the mine. I would rather leave the crew ready than stand beside a machine for pride.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What belongs in your handover notes?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The sound of a bit catching on fractured rock, with the hole number and a photograph. I would ask a junior operator to check the note beside the face. A fault list only matters if another person can use it.

say: I would ask for a **published test calendar** across the long warning.
I would leave **usable fault notes** for younger operators.
think: At about **seventy-one**, I expect retirement before capable robots if pension income holds.
Strong **savings** and yearly reviews support that choice.
do: **Keep** leading drills while writing apprentice fault notes.
**Request** an annual pension update before setting a final retirement date.
feel: **Calm** about household income and focused on a useful handover.
S4.quote: A fault list only matters if another person can use it.
fieldNote: The **2039 robot date** falls near age seventy-one, after likely retirement.
His **savings and pension** support calm, though he checks numbers yearly.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because capable robot drills could arrive around 2031 before our planned retirement. A real-rock trial and funded training tied to paid test posts would help. I would also want reliable pension figures.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who records a machine’s near misses before the first crew is cut. I have heard a drill bit catch where a neat plan showed clear rock. A good robot test needs the people who know that sound.

headlineQuote: I have heard a drill bit catch where a neat plan showed clear rock.
portrait: Ben Mensah is a **58-year-old** underground drill lead at Red Lantern mine, with a technical diploma and grown children.
He earns **higher pay**, has substantial savings and can look to several nearby mines as retirement approaches.
He uses **AI daily**, but tests new charts and risk maps against physical bits, rock and fault logs.
Fast robot availability makes him **anxious** about wages; longer warning lets him compare pension income and trial roles.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** worries him most because capable robot drills could arrive around 2031 before planned retirement.
whatWouldHelp: A **real-rock trial**, funded training tied to paid posts and reliable pension figures would help.
